e.t: This Greek LXX verb means “slumberless; sleepless.” It describes a person remaining awake rather than sleeping. The word can therefore refer simply to wakefulness, whether during a night of waiting, watching, or ordinary lack of sleep; the surrounding passage determines the particular reason. It occurs 10 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, so its central idea is consistent: being awake and not asleep.

Azouba, also rendered Azuva, is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs twice in the LXX corpus, once in 1 Kings 22:42 and once in 2 Chronicles 20:31. The available information establishes the name and its use as a proper noun, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain the identity or role of either person named.

This adverb means “unreasonably”: acting or speaking without a sound basis in reason. It describes the manner in which something is done, rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. Because it occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus represented here, its precise force in 4 Maccabees 6:14 depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included. Its basic sense remains clear: something is done in a way that disregards reasonable judgment.

This Greek LXX adjective describes something that is misshapen or unsightly—lacking a pleasing or well-formed appearance. It functions as a descriptive word, identifying how something looks rather than naming an object or action. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Wisdom 11:17. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its precise force in that passage must be understood from its immediate context. Its central meaning remains a description of unattractive or malformed appearance.

This verb means to relax, loosen, or release what is being held back. It can describe letting something go, easing restraint, or becoming less strict or forceful. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it occurs 39 times, so its precise sense depends on what is being relaxed or released in the sentence. The central idea remains a reduction of tension, restraint, or firmness rather than active strengthening or tightening.

Annon is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a word describing an action, quality, or object, but a personal designation. This name appears four times in the LXX, all within 2 Samuel 10:1–4. The supplied form and gloss both preserve the name as “Annon,” so its meaning is its identifying name rather than a separately defined descriptive term.

“Want of education” refers to a lack of learning or instruction. As a noun in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, it describes an absence of the teaching or formation a person needs. It is not simply a statement about intelligence; it points to being insufficiently taught. This word occurs four times in this LXX corpus: once in Hosea and three times in Sirach. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument.

This verb means to lament bitterly—to express deep grief in words or cries. It describes an intense outpouring of sorrow rather than a quiet feeling of sadness. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 4:12. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning is clear: bitter, deeply felt mourning.

This noun means “release” or “deliverance from,” naming freedom from something that restrains, burdens, threatens, or holds a person. In the Greek LXX corpus, it appears only twice, both in 3 Maccabees 6, at verses 37 and 40. Its central idea is liberation, though the surrounding verse determines what someone is being released from and how that deliverance is expressed. The word therefore points to freedom from a condition or danger, not merely movement from one place to another.

This Greek LXX verb means “love no more”: it describes the ending or withdrawal of affection toward someone. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. It occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Deuteronomy 15:7. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the cessation of love or affection. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that corpus.

ἀποχωρέω is a verb meaning “get away” or “depart.” It describes leaving a place or moving away from someone or something, rather than remaining present. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it appears three times: once in Jeremiah and twice in Maccabees. The basic idea remains simple: separation through departure. The precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

gl: melter of silver; worker in silver
d: melter of silver; worker in silver

e.t: This Greek LXX noun refers to a “melter of silver; worker in silver”—someone whose work involves processing or working with silver. As a noun, it identifies a person by his craft rather than expressing an action, quality, or abstract idea. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Wisdom 15:9. The word’s specific role in that verse must be understood from the surrounding passage.

Archabin is a proper name, referring to a person named Archabin. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs twice, both times in Jeremiah 42:2–3. Since the name itself identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or spiritual concept, its meaning is simply the personal designation Archabin. The surrounding verse text is needed to identify the person’s role in that passage.

This noun means “high-priesthood,” referring to the office or status held by a high priest. It describes the recognized priestly position rather than the individual who occupies it. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, the word occurs 13 times, chiefly in 1 and 2 Maccabees, with two occurrences in 4 Maccabees. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject being discussed.

Assyria is a proper name identifying Assyria. In this Greek LXX corpus, the word appears once, in 4 Maccabees 13:9. Its function is to name a specific entity rather than describe an action, quality, or relationship. The English rendering is “Assyria,” matching the word’s stated meaning. The surrounding passage is needed to explain the word’s precise significance in that verse.

This word means “unburied,” describing someone or something whose body has not received burial. It is an adjective, so it identifies a condition rather than an action: the person or body remains without burial. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 5:10. The word’s basic meaning is clear, while the surrounding verse would determine the particular force of that description in context.

This verb means “deepen”: to make something deeper or cause it to extend farther downward or inward. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, so its basic meaning is clear even though the particular force in each passage depends on the surrounding verse. The word appears in Psalms and Jeremiah, including three recorded passages in those books. Its ordinary sense remains focused on increasing depth, whether used for something physical or as an image of greater inward extent.

This noun refers to “sharp thorns”—prickly growths capable of causing pain or hindering someone. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Judges 8:16, so its normal meaning is represented by this single recorded use. The word identifies the thorns themselves rather than an action or quality. Its precise force in Judges 8:16 depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the basic picture is clear: pointed, painful thorn growth.

Basourōth, also rendered Vasuroth, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. Its exact referent cannot be identified from the lexical information alone. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 22:1. The name should therefore be read as a specific designation in that passage, with its precise reference determined by the surrounding verse and passage context.

This word is a proper name for a place, rendered “Bēthseedta” or “Vithseethta.” It is not a general description or action word, but a geographical name used to identify a particular location. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Judges 7:22. The supplied lexical information gives the name itself but does not provide further details about the place, so its precise significance must come from the surrounding passage and broader biblical context.

This noun means “means of living; substance”—what a person possesses or depends on for material support. It can refer broadly to one's livelihood or resources rather than to a particular object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 5:23, and is rendered “substance.” Its precise force in that verse belongs to the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to material means or possessions that sustain life.

Bokki, also rendered Vokki, is a proper name rather than an ordinary descriptive word. It identifies a person or named figure in the Greek Old Testament, although the available verse information does not provide enough context to describe that individual further. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Ezra 7:4. Its meaning is therefore the name itself: “Bokki” or “Vokki,” not a separate quality, action, or object.

“Gluttony” means excessive or uncontrolled indulgence in eating. It is a noun naming this kind of greedy appetite or overindulgence. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 1:3. The word’s basic meaning can be understood plainly as a consuming desire for food that exceeds proper restraint. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This Greek LXX verb means “farm.” It describes working land as a farmer, focusing on the practical activity of cultivating or tending the ground. The word appears twice in the represented LXX corpus: once in 1 Chronicles and once in 1 Maccabees. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the exact wording and emphasis in each passage must be understood from its context. Its basic sense remains the act of farming or cultivating land.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Gērsom” or “Yirsom.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Judges 18:30. Because it is a name, its basic function is to identify the individual named in that passage; the surrounding verse is needed to understand that person’s role in the account.

Gozan is a proper name preserved in English as “Gozan.” It identifies a named place in the Greek Old Testament rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual concept. The name occurs five times in this Greek Old Testament corpus, appearing in 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, and Isaiah. Its precise historical or geographic significance depends on the surrounding passages, but the word itself functions simply as the place-name Gozan.

This Greek LXX verb means to petition: to make a request or appeal to someone. It describes asking earnestly rather than merely mentioning a desire. The word occurs 44 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus, so it is used for repeated acts of asking across different settings. Its precise force in any verse depends on who is making the petition and whom they address.

This word means “counsel” or “deliberation”: thoughtful advice, planning, or considered discussion about what should be done. As a noun, it refers to the counsel itself rather than the person giving it or the act of carrying it out. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, it occurs five times, including passages in Psalms, Wisdom, and Sirach. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains carefully formed counsel or purposeful deliberation.

This Greek LXX noun refers to setting something in order or regulating it. It presents order as an arranged condition or a regulating activity, rather than naming a person or object. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 2 Maccabees 2:29. Since the verse text and surrounding passage are not available here, its precise emphasis in that occurrence must be determined from its context. Its central meaning remains orderly arrangement or regulation.

This verb means “spread with; sprinkled with.” It describes something being covered or treated by spreading or sprinkling another substance over it. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears only twice, both in Leviticus, so its normal sense is narrowly represented but clear from its definition. The word emphasizes the action or condition of having something spread or sprinkled upon it, while the surrounding verse identifies the substance and setting. [p03:word:lxx:L703637:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L703637:occurrences]

“Tenure of land in” refers to holding or possessing land as an established right. This noun describes land tenure rather than a temporary visit, movement, or simple location. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Leviticus 25:16. The wording points to recognized possession or holding of land, while the exact force of the term in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means “stoop down and peep in”—to bend low and look into something from above or outside. It describes a deliberate physical act of lowering oneself in order to see what is inside, rather than simply looking straight ahead. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs once, in Bel and the Dragon 1:40. Its exact force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse text.

This verb means to heed or listen to someone, expressing attentive reception of what is said. It can describe giving proper attention to a voice, message, or request rather than merely hearing sounds. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, it occurs 228 times, so it is a broadly used word for listening with regard and responsiveness. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX verb means “empty out.” It describes the action of removing what is inside something so that it becomes empty. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming an object, person, or quality. The word occurs 14 times in the Greek LXX, across 13 verses, so its central sense is established by repeated use in the Old Testament Greek corpus. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being emptied and the surrounding sentence.

Elōm, or Elom, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person or place in the Greek Old Testament translation. This name appears once in the LXX, at Joshua 19:48. Because no verse text or surrounding passage is available here, the name’s specific identification must be determined from that passage itself; its lexical meaning is simply the proper name Elom.

This noun means “want” or “need,” referring to a condition in which something necessary is lacking. It names the state of need rather than an action, person, or object. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 19 times, showing a recurring vocabulary for lack or necessity. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This adjective describes something as active, functioning, or currently at work. Its central idea is that the activity is taking place rather than remaining inactive. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Ezekiel 46:1, and is rendered “working.” The surrounding verse is needed to explain exactly what is described there, but the word itself points plainly to present activity or operation.

This Greek word means “place”: it expresses the action of putting or setting something in a particular position. As a verb, it describes an instruction or act of positioning rather than a place itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Ezra 7:17 and Amos 7:8. Its exact force in either passage depends on what is being placed and the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the deliberate act of setting something where it belongs.

This verb means “quite enough for” or “suffice for”: it describes something being adequate or sufficient for a need. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, at Numbers 11:23, so its normal lexical sense is clear even though the verse’s particular force depends on the surrounding passage. The word expresses adequacy—something being enough to meet what is required—rather than merely describing abundance or excess.

“Visitation” is the meaning of this noun. It refers to a visitation or coming to someone, with the surrounding passage determining the particular force in each occurrence. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it appears three times: once in Judges, once in Proverbs, and once in Wisdom. Its basic meaning remains the same across these occurrences, while the immediate context explains what the visitation involves.

This Greek LXX verb means “send forth” or “send to war.” It describes the act of dispatching people or forces, especially when they are sent out for conflict. The word occurs four times in the LXX material represented here, in four verses across 2 Maccabees and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This verb means “have come back” or “return.” It describes going back to a previous place, person, or situation rather than remaining away. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it appears five times, including uses in Leviticus, Proverbs, and Sirach. The wording can describe a return that has happened or is expected to happen, depending on the sentence. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Greek verb means to come to someone’s aid or provide help when assistance is needed. It describes an active response—moving toward another person’s need rather than merely feeling concern. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs four times, all in 1–2 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains focused on giving practical support or rescue, while the surrounding passage determines who is helped and what form that aid takes.

This noun means “rebuke” or “reproof”: a spoken expression of correction or disapproval directed toward someone. It names the act or statement of confronting what is considered wrong, rather than describing the person who receives it. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 7:33. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain its precise force there.

This verb means to overshadow: to cover, cast a shadow over, or extend over something. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears four times, including passages in Exodus, Psalms, and Proverbs. Its exact force can be literal or figurative depending on the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains one thing coming over or covering another. The word is rendered “overshadow” in one recorded translation, supporting this straightforward sense.

This Greek LXX verb means “idle; unemployed.” It describes a person who is not working or engaged in useful activity. The word focuses on a condition of inactivity rather than naming a specific kind of work or explaining why someone is inactive. It occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Ezra 4:24. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the condition of being without work or activity.

This noun means “service done” or “kindness”—a beneficial act performed for someone else. It describes a deed viewed as helpful and generous, rather than merely an inward attitude or intention. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 5:20. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain how this word functions in that particular sentence, but its basic sense centers on a kindness expressed through practical service.

This Greek LXX noun means “area,” referring generally to a defined or available stretch of space. It is a spatial word rather than a description of a person, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 26:22. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense remains a place with room or extent. This word should therefore be understood simply as a reference to an area or open space.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Hēli” or “Ili.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 36 times across 32 verses, with most occurrences in 1 Samuel. Its precise reference in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic function remains that of a personal name.

Thamnathares is a proper name, referring to a specifically named person, place, or other entity rather than expressing a general idea or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Judges 2:9, and is rendered “Thamnathares.” The available lexical information identifies the name but does not specify what kind of entity bears it. Its precise referent therefore depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Thekoum, also rendered Thekum, is a proper name. It identifies a specific named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. Because it is a name, its meaning is primarily its identification of the person or place designated in the passage, not a broader descriptive concept. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, at Joshua 15:59.

This Greek LXX verb means “crush”: to press, break, or destroy something with force. It describes an action rather than a person or thing. The word occurs 19 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, appearing across passages translated from several biblical settings. Its exact force—whether physical breaking or the destruction of an opponent—depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains forceful crushing.

Iason is a proper name identifying a person, rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It is rendered “Iasōn; Iason” and functions as a personal name in the Greek LXX corpus. This name occurs 15 times, across 15 verses, with most occurrences in 2 Maccabees. Its significance in any particular passage depends on which person named Iason is being discussed there.

This word is a personal name, rendered as “Iedeiou” or “Iethiu.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 12:21. Because the available information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, its specific role in that passage cannot be stated more precisely. The name itself should therefore be understood as a proper name identifying a person.

Iexan, also rendered Ieksan, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament tradition. The name occurs four times in the LXX corpus, appearing in Genesis and 1 Chronicles. Because a personal name normally identifies someone rather than defining a concept, its basic meaning here is simply the person's name: Iexan or Ieksan.

This word is a proper name rendered “Iesbi” or “Iezvi.” It identifies a named individual or figure rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Samuel 21:16. The available lexical information gives the name’s recognized renderings but does not provide an additional definition or explain the person’s role. Its precise significance in that passage must therefore be understood from the surrounding verse and narrative context.

This adjective describes something with an even surface—flat, level, or made equal in height. It can refer to physical ground or another surface that has no significant rise or unevenness. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs three times, all in the deuterocanonical books of 2 and 3 Maccabees. Its central idea remains consistent: a surface or area brought to, or existing at, an even level. The exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means to confess—to openly acknowledge or admit something. It describes an act of speaking honestly rather than merely holding an opinion inwardly. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears twice, both times in Exodus 21, so its recorded use is limited to that passage. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording and situation, but the central idea remains a spoken confession or acknowledgment.

This noun means “descent”: a going down or downward movement. It can describe the act or direction of moving from a higher place to a lower one. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented here, it occurs 11 times, so its basic meaning is established across several passages without being limited to one setting. The word appears in Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings, Sirach, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

gl: give as an inheritance; parcel out
d: give as an inheritance; parcel out

e.t: This LXX verb means to give something as an inheritance or to parcel it out. It describes the act of assigning or distributing what is to be received as a possession, especially when an inheritance is being allotted. The word occurs twice in the LXX corpus represented here, once in Deuteronomy and once in 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is the deliberate granting or dividing of an inheritance.

Slander means harmful or false speech directed against another person. As a noun, it names the act or substance of speaking against someone in a damaging way. This Greek LXX word has one recorded occurrence, in Wisdom 1:11, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic meaning remains clear: speech that attacks another person’s reputation rather than communicating truth or goodwill.

gl: form a counter-party in the state
d: form a counter-party in the state

e.t: This verb means to “form a counter-party in the state,” describing the action of establishing an opposing party within a state. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than a person, place, or object. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Exodus 38:22. The available wording identifies its general lexical sense, while the precise force of the action in that verse belongs to its surrounding context.

This verb means to exult over someone—to take joy or triumph in that person’s downfall or distress. It describes an active response rather than a general feeling, expressing gladness directed against another. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 1:26. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse text, but the word itself focuses on celebrating another person’s trouble rather than simply experiencing personal happiness.

This Greek LXX noun means a twig or spray—a small branch or leafy offshoot of a plant. It refers to a physical part of vegetation rather than an action or abstract idea. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related Wisdom literature, appearing twice in Job and once in Wisdom. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and imagery, but its basic sense remains a small branch, sprig, or spray.

This LXX Greek verb means “hide”: to put someone or something out of sight, or to conceal it from notice. It describes an action rather than a person or object. The word occurs 133 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, showing that concealment is its consistent lexical sense across many passages. The surrounding verse determines whether the hiding is for protection, secrecy, or another purpose; the word itself simply expresses hiding or concealing.

This Greek LXX word means “circling” or “from all around.” It describes movement, position, or direction surrounding something rather than coming from only one side. As an adverb or preposition, it can indicate that something happens around an object or comes from every direction. The word occurs 90 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, so its basic idea is used broadly for surrounding movement or location.

Kōladam, also rendered Kolatham, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named person, place, or other entity, but the available lexical information does not specify which kind. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Joshua 19:2. Its precise referent is determined by the surrounding verse and passage rather than by the name itself.

This Greek LXX verb means “lick up”: to gather or consume something with the tongue. It describes a physical action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament, across four verses, including passages in 1 Kings, Psalms, Isaiah, and Micah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains the act of licking something up.

This Greek LXX verb means to pray or entreat—to address a plea to God or another person. It describes earnest asking rather than a casual statement. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here: once in Psalms and once in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and its subject, but its central idea remains a prayerful or urgent appeal.

Lotan is a personal name, not a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX, it identifies a person named Lotan in genealogical lists. The name occurs six times across five verses, in Genesis 36 and 1 Chronicles 1. Its normal function is to distinguish this individual from other names in those family records. No separate common-word sense is indicated here.

Madian, also rendered Mathian, is a proper name used in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named biblical entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs 62 times across 57 verses, from Genesis through Habakkuk, with especially frequent use in Judges and additional occurrences in Numbers and Exodus. Its exact reference—whether to a people, territory, or another named subject—depends on the surrounding verse, but the lexical meaning itself is the name “Madian; Mathian.”

This noun means an abomination: something viewed as morally or religiously detestable and therefore unacceptable. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both in Ezra 9, referring to what is condemned as abominable. The word identifies the offending thing itself rather than an action or feeling. Its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage and immediate context.

Methla is a proper name preserved in the Greek Septuagint text. It is not presented here as a common word describing an action, quality, or object, but as a personal or place name whose precise referent must be identified from the surrounding passage. The name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at Judges 20:48, and is rendered “Methla.”

Meinōm is a proper name, identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, or idea. It is also represented as Minom. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Nehemiah 7:52. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s precise role in that passage cannot be described further. Its basic meaning is therefore its function as a personal name: it distinguishes one individual within the account.

This Greek LXX verb means “regret”: to feel sorrow or dissatisfaction about something previously done, chosen, or experienced. It describes a change of feeling toward an earlier action or decision, rather than merely recognizing what happened. The word occurs 14 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its exact force depends on the surrounding passage. As a verb, it expresses what a person does inwardly—regretting something—rather than naming the sorrow itself. Its established meaning is concise: regret.

Noum, also rendered Num, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 7:27. The available wording identifies the person by name but does not provide enough verse text or surrounding context to explain anything further about that individual. Its meaning is therefore best understood as the personal name Noum or Num in this LXX passage.

Ozaza is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament, identifying a particular person or name-bearing figure rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The available lexical definition is simply “Ozaza,” so no broader meaning should be added to it. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at 1 Chronicles 2:33. Its significance in that passage depends on the surrounding genealogy and verse text.

This word means “administrator”: a person entrusted to manage a household, estate, or other responsibility. It is a noun describing someone who oversees what belongs to another and carries out that trust faithfully. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 12 times across 12 verses, especially in historical accounts and Isaiah. The word therefore points to a responsible manager, not merely someone who performs a task. Its precise role in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This adjective describes someone or something “able to see” or “observant.” It points to the capacity to perceive clearly, whether by sight or attentive awareness. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs only once, in Proverbs 22:29. Because no verse text or surrounding context is available here, the word’s particular force in that passage cannot be stated beyond this basic meaning. Its use is adjectival, describing a quality rather than naming an action or person.

This Greek LXX noun means “impulse,” referring to an inward drive or powerful urge that moves someone toward action. It describes force arising within a person rather than merely an outward event. The word occurs ten times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here, including passages from Numbers, Proverbs, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains a compelling inner movement or drive.

This noun refers to “all the herbage; grass”—the vegetation that covers the ground. It is a general word for plant growth rather than the name of one particular plant. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 5:25. That reference identifies its only recorded use, while the word’s basic meaning remains the broad idea of grass or herbage. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This verb means to enrage or provoke—to stir someone to anger or resentment. It describes an action that arouses strong displeasure rather than merely causing ordinary irritation. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used 49 times, especially in passages describing actions that provoke God. Its basic sense remains active: someone causes another to become angry. The precise force in any verse depends on its surrounding context.

This verb describes sound spreading around or echoing. It refers to a noise that carries through an area and can be heard as it resounds. The central idea is not simply making a sound, but sound surrounding or reverberating through a place. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in the deuterocanonical book of Wisdom. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is sound that travels around and echoes.

This Greek LXX verb means “leave around”: to leave something remaining or positioned around something else. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX material represented here, appearing twice in 2 Maccabees and twice in 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular sentence depends on what is being left and the surrounding context.

e.t: This Greek LXX verb means “make a false note in music”: it describes producing a wrong or discordant note rather than a true one. As a verb, it names an action, not a person or object. The musical image gives the word its central sense—an action that misses the proper note. It occurs 32 times across the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented here, while its precise force in a verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This verb means to long for or yearn after someone or something. It describes an inward desire directed toward what a person strongly wants, seeks, or misses. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs seven times, including passages from Esther, Proverbs, and Wisdom. Its precise force in any one verse depends on what the surrounding sentence identifies as the object of longing.

This Greek LXX verb means “prepare in advance”: to make something ready beforehand. It describes an action carried out ahead of the time when it will be needed, rather than merely beginning preparation at the last moment. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus, once in Isaiah and once in Wisdom. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains arranging or making ready beforehand. It is an action word, so it describes what someone does rather than an object or quality.

This verb means “have arrived at,” describing reaching a point, place, or stage. It presents arrival as something already accomplished rather than an action still underway. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, once in 2 Maccabees and once in 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains that something has reached the relevant destination or point.

This word means “heel,” referring to the rear part of the foot. It is a noun used for that body part in the LXX corpus. The word occurs nine times, including passages in Genesis, Joshua, Judges, and Psalms. Its basic meaning remains concrete and consistent: a heel or the heels. The surrounding verse determines what is being said about the heel in each occurrence.

This noun refers to a “stream” or “drain”—a channel through which water flows away or is carried off. It describes a physical watercourse rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 40:40. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain its specific architectural or situational role there, but its ordinary meaning is a stream or drainage channel.

Salmana is a proper name, referring to a specific person rather than expressing a general quality, action, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Psalms 82:12, and is rendered “Salmana.” The available wording identifies the name but does not provide an additional ordinary meaning or description. Its precise significance in that verse must therefore be understood from the surrounding passage, not from the name alone.

“Saour” is a proper name, referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears once, at 1 Chronicles 4:5. It is presented in the available lexical information as “Saour” and “Saur,” two English representations of the same personal name. Because no verse text or wider context is available here, the name itself does not provide a further meaning beyond identifying its bearer.

This verb means to venerate someone or to stand in awe of that person. It describes an attitude of deep respect and reverence, especially toward one regarded as worthy of honor. As a verb, it expresses the act of showing this reverence rather than merely naming the feeling. In the Greek Old Testament and related books represented here, it occurs 20 times, showing that it can describe a recurring response of honor toward God or other revered figures. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

Seppharim, also called Sepfarim, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an idea or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in Isaiah: once in Isaiah 36:19 and again in Isaiah 37:13. Because it is a place or people name in the passage, its identity and significance depend on the surrounding verse and historical setting, not on a broader dictionary sense.

Somoron is a proper name, rendered “Somoron” (also “Somorōn”), rather than an ordinary word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs five times in four verses. The available lexical information identifies the name but does not provide a further definition or explain its referent; its specific significance in any verse must come from that passage’s surrounding text.

This adjective means “narrow” or “strait,” describing something limited in width or space. It can refer to a physically constricted place or passage, and its exact force depends on the noun and sentence where it appears. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 15 times, including passages in 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 2 Kings, Isaiah, and Baruch. The word therefore carries a consistent basic idea of restricted room or limited breadth rather than openness or expansiveness.

“Arcade” describes an architectural passage or walkway, typically formed or bordered by a row of arches or columns. It is a noun naming a built feature rather than an action, person, or abstract quality. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), this word occurs four times: once in 1 Kings and three times in Ezekiel. Its precise architectural arrangement in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and setting.

This Greek LXX verb means to place someone beside another person also. It describes bringing or setting one person alongside another, with the added sense that this happens as well. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Psalm 93:16. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning centers on positioning someone beside another rather than simply placing something anywhere.

The word means “burnt together.” It is a verb describing people or things being consumed by fire as one, with the idea of burning collectively rather than separately. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 6:11. That single occurrence confirms its rarity in this corpus, but the word’s basic meaning remains straightforward: it expresses being burned together. The precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, which is not included here.

This noun means “completeness” or “accomplishment.” It points to something brought to its intended finish, viewed as complete rather than lacking what is needed. The word appears four times in this Greek Scripture corpus: twice in Judges and twice in Wisdom. Those occurrences show that it can speak of a completed state or achieved result, while the surrounding sentence determines its precise emphasis in each passage.

This word means “forty,” naming a specific quantity or number. It functions as an indeclinable number adjective, usually indicating that something is forty in amount, count, or measure. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 133 times, so it is a common numerical term rather than a rare or specialized expression. Its normal meaning remains the straightforward number forty; the significance of a particular occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek LXX particle means “actually.” It adds emphasis to a statement, drawing attention to what is true or genuinely the case. Rather than naming a person, object, action, or quality, it modifies the force of nearby words in a sentence. The word occurs eight times in the Greek LXX corpus represented here, all in 4 Maccabees. Its exact emphasis in any particular verse is determined by the surrounding sentence, but its basic function is to underscore or affirm what is being said.

This Greek LXX noun means “archer”: a person who shoots arrows with a bow. It identifies someone by this military or hunting skill rather than describing an action or quality. The word occurs nine times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing across Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its use includes both singular and plural references, while retaining the same basic meaning of a person or group of people who use bows in combat or shooting.

This noun refers to a hyaena, a wild animal. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 13:18. The word identifies the animal itself rather than an action, quality, or abstract idea. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning is simply hyaena. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that corpus rather than treated as a Greek New Testament occurrence.

This noun means “covering with a shield; protection.” It describes the safety or defense provided by shielding someone from danger, like a shield placed between a person and an attack. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times, including passages from 2 Samuel, Psalms, Lamentations, and Sirach. Its central idea is protective covering rather than the shield as merely an object. The surrounding verse determines whether the word emphasizes the act of shielding or the protection received.

This Greek Old Testament noun means “gorge,” referring to a deep, narrow passage or valley in the land. It is a physical geographical term, used for named or recognizable land formations rather than an abstract idea. The word occurs 80 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical material, so it describes a recurring feature of the biblical landscape. Its exact reference in any verse depends on the surrounding place description, but its central meaning remains a gorge or ravine.

Phesēchi, also rendered Fesikhi, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament and occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 7:33. The available information preserves the name itself but does not provide a separate definition or explanation of its meaning. Its significance in that genealogy comes from identifying the individual named there, while the surrounding verse supplies the specific family context.

This verb describes something being “soaked” or “mixed,” especially when material becomes thoroughly saturated or combined. It appears seven times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical books, including passages in Job, Isaiah, Ezekiel, and 3 Maccabees. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on becoming wet, being blended, or undergoing a similar combining process. Its basic sense concerns material changed through contact with or combination with something else.

This verb means “bereaved,” describing someone who has suffered the loss of a loved one. It focuses on the condition produced by that loss rather than naming the person who died. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs only twice, showing a specific word used in two recorded passages rather than a broad, frequently repeated term. Its occurrences are found in 2 Samuel 13:20 and Jeremiah 28:5. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain the particular situation in either passage.

This LXX verb means “miscarry,” describing a pregnancy that fails to result in birth. It functions as an action word rather than a name or description of a person. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Job 21:10, so its normal lexical meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. Its precise force in that passage belongs to the context of the verse and its surrounding statements.

This word means “just as” and functions as an adverb that compares one statement, action, or circumstance with another. It introduces a likeness or correspondence, helping connect ideas by showing that something happens in the same way as something else. It appears 259 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, so it is a common word for drawing comparisons. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.
